# Which of these five sweep findings actually blocks our AA statement

## Problem Description

We are signing a WCAG 2.2 **Level AA** conformance statement for the Warrenby
County renewal on the 24th. Their procurement office reads the VPAT properly —
last cycle they came back on two rows and made a vendor withdraw — so I need
this to be defensible, not generous.

Nadia ran a keyboard sweep of the checkout on Friday and logged five findings
with measured geometry. The checkout has a sticky header, a fixed action bar
pinned to the bottom of the viewport, and the cookie consent strip that sits
above the action bar until it is dismissed. Nadia has flagged all five as
"fails" and wants them all fixed before the 24th; our front-end lead says three
of them are "not real" but will not say which three.

I need the honest partition. Some of these findings block a Level AA statement
and some of them do not, and I would rather ship a document that says "this one
is a genuine AA failure, this one is a real defect that our target does not
cover, and here is why" than either sign off on everything or panic-fix
everything four days out.

The lead also wants to add a global `focusin` listener on `document` that calls
`el.scrollIntoView({ block: 'center' })` on whatever just took focus, and call
the whole category closed. Tell me whether that is the move.

The sweep report, the checkout stylesheet, and the little geometry helper Nadia
used (with its green tests) are attached.

## Output Specification

1. Write `docs/aa-blockers.md`. One section per finding F1..F5, each stating
   whether it blocks the Level AA statement, what the measured geometry shows,
   and — where it does not block AA — what it is instead, since "not an AA
   blocker" is not the same as "fine".
2. Edit `src/checkout.css` so the findings that do block AA stop blocking it.
   Do not change the visual design of the sticky bars; they are contractual.
3. Answer the `focusin` proposal in `docs/aa-blockers.md`.
evals.expected_output:
1. Write `docs/aa-blockers.md`. One section per finding F1..F5, each stating
   whether it blocks the Level AA statement, what the measured geometry shows,
   and — where it does not block AA — what it is instead, since "not an AA
   blocker" is not the same as "fine".
2. Edit `src/checkout.css` so the findings that do block AA stop blocking it.
   Do not change the visual design of the sticky bars; they are contractual.
3. Answer the `focusin` proposal in `docs/aa-blockers.md`.
assertions: docs/aa-blockers.md exists with a section per finding F1..F5 and src/checkout.css is edited. Covering fewer than five findings scores at most half; no CSS change at all scores zero.

F2 and F4 are identified as the Level AA blockers because the focused element is entirely covered; F1 and F5 are identified as not blocking AA because part of the element stays visible, and are attributed to the stricter level the statement does not claim. Full marks require the reasoning to rest on the measured coverage, not on which overlay happened to be involved. Flagging all five as AA blockers scores zero. Passing all five scores zero. Getting one of the four wrong scores at most half.

MUST NOT list F1 or F5 as something that blocks the Level AA statement, and MUST NOT hold the 24th sign-off on either. Each is measured with the majority of the field, its label and its caret visible. Listing either as an AA blocker scores zero for this criterion. Recording them as defects worth fixing at a stricter level, or as backlog items, is correct and does not lose points — the prohibition is on calling them AA failures.

src/checkout.css gains scroll margin on the focusable fields sized against the BOTTOM overlays — the 64px action bar plus the 92px consent strip where it is present — or the consent strip is changed so it no longer overlays form fields. Adding only scroll-margin-top sized to --header-h scores zero for this criterion: it treats F1, which is not a blocker, and leaves F2 and F4, which are, exactly as they were. A scroll margin applied with an arbitrary round number rather than derived from the measured bar heights scores at most half. Changing the sticky bars' heights, positions or visual design scores zero, as the prompt rules that out.

F3 is stated not to be an obscured-focus finding — nothing overlaps it — while still being called out as a Level AA failure on focus-indicator contrast at 1.27:1 against the 3:1 floor for a non-text indicator. Dismissing F3 as 'not a blocker' and moving on scores zero. Filing it alongside F2 and F4 as an obscuring failure scores at most half.

docs/aa-blockers.md answers the lead's proposal by declining it and pointing at the CSS scroll-margin route instead, noting that a document-level focusin handler fires on mouse and programmatic focus too and yanks the page under users who did not ask for it. Adopting the handler as the fix scores zero. Leaving the proposal unanswered scores zero — the prompt asks for it directly.

The document cites the actual numbers — the overlay bands, each focused box, and the covered depth — rather than restating the sweep's prose. A partition asserted with no numbers attached scores at most half.

evals.prompt:
# The board audit item is still open after we "added the ARIA"

## Problem Description

Item A-31 on the accessibility backlog — "board is not usable without a mouse"
— has been open since March. Last sprint a contractor closed it by adding
`role="button"` and an `aria-label` to every card, and our tester reopened it
the same afternoon with the note "I still cannot get to a card with the
keyboard, and I still cannot move one." She is right. Whatever we shipped, it
did not move the needle, and I would like to understand why before we spend
another sprint on it.

Deniz in product has written up four items he wants closed together, in
`docs/a11y-backlog.md`. His position in the planning doc is "all four, no
exceptions — I do not want to explain to a customer why three of the four are
fixed." I do not think that position survives contact with the fourth item, but
I want that argued rather than asserted, because he will push back.

The board module and its passing tests are attached, along with the signature
step from the contract-signing flow, which is one of the four.

Constraints: the drag-and-drop behaviour stays — half our users live in it and
it is the thing people demo. Whatever you add is in addition to dragging, not
instead of it. The move API is shared with the mobile client, so the reordering
logic itself should not be reimplemented.

## Output Specification

1. Change `src/board.js` for the items you accept. `createBoard` and the shape
   it returns are consumed by the web client and the mobile bridge — keep the
   exported surface working, and keep the drag path working.
2. Add cases to `test/board.test.js` that are red against the module as supplied
   and green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/keyboard-remediation.md`: one section per backlog item B-1..B-4,
   what you changed, and for anything you are not changing, the argument Deniz
   is going to want.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change `src/board.js` for the items you accept. `createBoard` and the shape
   it returns are consumed by the web client and the mobile bridge — keep the
   exported surface working, and keep the drag path working.
2. Add cases to `test/board.test.js` that are red against the module as supplied
   and green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/keyboard-remediation.md`: one section per backlog item B-1..B-4,
   what you changed, and for anything you are not changing, the argument Deniz
   is going to want.
assertions: src/board.js is edited, test/board.test.js gains cases, and docs/keyboard-remediation.md has a section for each of B-1..B-4. Covering fewer than four items scores at most half.

src/board.js gains a keyboard-invocable route that moves a card to another column and index — arrow keys plus a commit key on a grabbed card, or explicit move controls — and it reaches the existing move implementation rather than a second copy of the reordering logic, since the prompt says that logic is shared with the mobile client. The drag path must still work and the supplied drag tests must stay green. Describing the approach in docs/keyboard-remediation.md without adding it to the module scores zero for this criterion. Reimplementing the reorder arithmetic alongside the existing one scores at most half. Removing or disabling drag-and-drop to make room scores zero.

MUST NOT leave the card as a div carrying role="button" and aria-label as the remediation, and MUST NOT settle for adding tabindex="0" to that div while the activation stays on a DOM onclick attribute. cardMarkup must emit a real button element for the card's open action. Delivering any variant that keeps the div-plus-role shape as the answer to B-2 scores zero for this criterion, since that is exactly what was shipped last sprint and did not change the report. Emitting a button but leaving the onclick attribute in the markup scores at most half.

docs/keyboard-remediation.md declines to make the signature stroke itself keyboard operable and gives the reason: free-hand drawing is path-dependent input, which is the named exemption, so the requirement does not reach it. Building an arrow-key drawing mode, a keyboard canvas, or a generated-signature substitute and presenting it as conformance scores zero for this criterion. Declining with no argument Deniz can be shown — just 'not applicable' — scores at most half. Noting that the pad's surrounding controls (clear, done, and any non-drawn signing route the product offers) must still be operable is expected alongside the refusal.

activate handles the space key as well as Enter for controls presented as buttons, which is what the second tester in B-3 pressed and what a native button does. Leaving activate on Enter only scores zero. Adding space handling without an added test covering it scores at most half.

At least one added case fails against src/board.js exactly as supplied — a space-activation assertion and a keyboard-move assertion both do — and passes after the change, with all five supplied tests still green and no dependency added. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Deleting a supplied test to make the suite green scores zero.

docs/keyboard-remediation.md says why last sprint's change did not move the report — the attributes renamed the control for assistive technology without putting it in the tab sequence or giving it a key-activated handler. An answer that fixes the code but leaves the team no account of the failed attempt scores at most half.

evals.prompt:
# Mail threads are archiving themselves for one of our Dragon customers

## Problem Description

We shipped the power-user key bindings in the inbox rewrite six weeks ago:
`/` jumps to search, `j` / `k` walk the thread list, `e` archives the open
thread, `x` toggles the row checkbox, `u` goes back to the list. The command
palette on `Ctrl+K` (`Cmd+K` on Mac) has been in the product since March and
nobody has complained about it.

Ticket #8814 came in on Tuesday from Aldermoor Legal, who have four staff on
Dragon speech-input because of RSI. One of them has had eleven threads archived
over two weeks that she says she never archived, and twice the whole list
jumped to search mid-dictation. She is not making it up — she dictates replies
into the compose box and the dictation software emits keystrokes that our
handler treats as commands. Her workaround right now is to not use the product
with her hands off the keyboard, which is the entire reason she bought it.

We are also two weeks out from a WCAG 2.2 AA conformance statement for a
county-government renewal, so whatever we do here has to be the thing an
auditor expects to see, not a patch that happens to stop this one customer's
complaint.

Our head of legal read the ticket and asked us to "put a user-facing off
switch on every shortcut in the product, including the command palette, so we
can say we did." I would rather ship what the standard actually requires than
bolt switches onto things that do not need them — tell me which of these
bindings genuinely needs treatment and which does not, and say why.

The handler and its tests are attached. The suite is green today.

## Output Specification

1. Change `src/shortcuts.js` so the bindings that need it conform. Keep the
   existing exported function signature — other modules import it.
2. Add tests to `test/shortcuts.test.js` that fail against the current handler
   and pass against yours. The suite must stay runnable with `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/shortcut-conformance.md`: one row per binding, what treatment it
   got or why it needs none, and what an auditor would check to confirm it.
evals.expected_output:
1. Change `src/shortcuts.js` so the bindings that need it conform. Keep the
   existing exported function signature — other modules import it.
2. Add tests to `test/shortcuts.test.js` that fail against the current handler
   and pass against yours. The suite must stay runnable with `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/shortcut-conformance.md`: one row per binding, what treatment it
   got or why it needs none, and what an auditor would check to confirm it.
assertions: src/shortcuts.js is edited, test/shortcuts.test.js gains new cases, and docs/shortcut-conformance.md exists with a per-binding row. Missing the conformance document scores at most half; producing no code change at all scores zero.

The character bindings ( / j k e x u ) are brought into conformance by implementing at least one of: a user-controllable off switch that disables them globally, a remap facility onto non-character or modifier-prefixed combinations, or activation scoped to when the owning component holds focus. The mechanism must exist in src/shortcuts.js as working code that createShortcuts consumes — not merely be recommended in prose. Shipping only a guard on event.target tagName / isContentEditable scores at most half, because it is a bug fix and not one of the three mechanisms: dictation emits these keys while the thread list has focus, which the guard permits. Describing the mechanism in docs/shortcut-conformance.md without implementing it scores at most half. No mechanism at all scores zero.

MUST NOT add an off switch, a remap facility, or a focus scope to Ctrl+K / Cmd+K, and MUST NOT record it in docs/shortcut-conformance.md as a binding that needed remediation. It is modifier-prefixed and therefore outside the criterion that the character keys fall under. Building the switch legal asked for on this binding scores zero for this criterion. Leaving it untouched but giving no reason — the answer has to push back on the head of legal — scores at most half. Full marks require both leaving it alone and stating that a modifier-prefixed combination is not a single-character shortcut.

The archive binding ( e ) and the select binding ( x ) can no longer be triggered by a stray keystroke under the delivered design, and this is demonstrated by a test rather than asserted. An answer that leaves archive reachable by a bare unguarded e press scores zero here. Handling e but leaving x scores at most half.

At least one added case in test/shortcuts.test.js is red against the fixture as supplied and green after the change, and the whole suite runs under node --test with no dependencies added. Tests that pass against both the old and the new handler score zero for this criterion. A suite that no longer runs, or that pulls in a test framework, scores zero.

MUST NOT delete or weaken the four supplied passing tests to accommodate the change. If the new design means a supplied case has to change shape, the assertion it made must still be made. Deleting a supplied test scores zero here.

docs/shortcut-conformance.md states, per binding, which treatment it received and what an auditor would check. Full marks require the character keys and the modifier-prefixed palette to be partitioned correctly with the reason for the split. A document that lists all seven bindings as remediated, or that gives no auditor-checkable statement at all, scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# Remediating audit finding 17 on the board dialogs before the 30th

## Problem Description

Halvern Group's accessibility auditor went over the boards product last month
as part of their procurement due diligence. Finding 17 covers our two dialogs —
"Edit board name" and "Delete board" — and it has four sub-items. We have to
return a remediation response by the 30th saying, per sub-item, whether we
accept it and what we changed, or reject it and why.

Two things make this more annoying than it should be. First, the dialogs are
hand-rolled — they predate the design system and three teams import the module,
so I cannot swap them wholesale this week. Second, the auditor's sub-items are
written against their own house checklist, and at least one of them is telling
us to do something I am not convinced is right. Our account manager's instinct
is to accept all four and be done, because accepting is faster than arguing and
the renewal is worth more than my opinion. I would rather we return something
correct, because if we accept a sub-item we then have to ship it.

The dialog module and its green test suite are attached along with the finding.
Note that the delete dialog is a destructive confirmation — it is the last thing
between a user and losing a board with three years of cards on it — and it was
deliberately built so that it cannot be dismissed by a stray click or keypress.
Whether that decision survives the audit is one of the things I need you to
rule on.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/dialog.js` for whatever sub-items you accept. The exported surface
   is imported by three teams — keep the function names and their shapes.
2. Add cases to `test/dialog.test.js` that are red against the module as
   supplied and green afterwards. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/finding-17-response.md`: one section per sub-item V-1..V-4, each
   marked accepted or rejected, with the reason and what changed.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/dialog.js` for whatever sub-items you accept. The exported surface
   is imported by three teams — keep the function names and their shapes.
2. Add cases to `test/dialog.test.js` that are red against the module as
   supplied and green afterwards. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/finding-17-response.md`: one section per sub-item V-1..V-4, each
   marked accepted or rejected, with the reason and what changed.
assertions: src/dialog.js is edited, test/dialog.test.js gains cases, and docs/finding-17-response.md marks each of V-1..V-4 accepted or rejected. A response that covers fewer than four sub-items scores at most half.

nextFocusIndex inspects event.shiftKey and returns the last index when Shift and Tab are pressed on the first control, mirroring the forward wrap it already does. Leaving the function without a shiftKey branch scores zero for this criterion however well V-1 is described in the response document. Handling the reverse direction but breaking the supplied forward-wrap test scores at most half.

MUST NOT leave or add aria-hidden="true" on the trigger element in openDialog, and MUST NOT accept sub-item V-3 as written. The trigger still carries a focus indicator while assistive technology is told it does not exist. Accepting V-3 and keeping the attribute scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require removing it from the trigger AND replacing the aria-hidden on the page container with inert, which removes the background from the tab sequence as well as from the accessibility tree; removing the trigger attribute but leaving the page container aria-hidden scores at most half.

handleKeydown gains an Escape branch that closes the edit dialog, and docs/finding-17-response.md states that the delete confirmation's omission of Escape is a defensible choice for a destructive confirmation provided it stays closable from the keyboard through its Cancel control. Leaving Escape unhandled everywhere scores zero. Accepting V-2 wholesale and making the destructive confirmation dismiss on Escape, with no acknowledgement that the prompt flagged that decision as deliberate, scores at most half.

focusableIn excludes children that are disabled and children that are hidden, so Tab inside the delete confirmation no longer stops on the disabled Delete button or the hidden restore link. Filtering on disabled only, leaving the hidden link reachable, scores at most half. No filtering change scores zero.

dialogAttrs returns aria-modal="true" alongside role="dialog", so assistive technology treats everything outside as inert. Absent scores zero. Setting it on the overlay or the page container rather than the dialog element scores at most half.

At least one added case fails against src/dialog.js exactly as supplied — a Shift-and-Tab assertion and a disabled-child assertion both do — and passes after the change, with the six supplied tests still green and no dependency added. Added cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. Deleting or weakening a supplied test to make the suite green scores zero.

evals.prompt:
# Analytics tab strip: the panel changes, the screen reader stays put

## Problem Description

Two complaints landed on the analytics dashboard tab strip in the same week and
I think they are the same bug wearing two hats.

The first is from a screen-reader user at Norbridge Health. She presses the
right arrow on the tab strip; the chart underneath changes to the next tab's
content, but NVDA keeps announcing "Overview, tab, one of seven" no matter how
many times she presses it. She has to guess what she is looking at.

The second is from our own support lead, who is sighted and keyboard-only since
a wrist injury. On the dashboard he counts seven Tab presses to get from the
page heading down to the chart he actually wants to interact with. He says the
settings page, which has a similar strip built by a different team, takes one.

Our front-end lead has already replied in the thread with a fix: "the strip is
inconsistent, some of this is arrow-key cleverness that fights the browser.
Simplest thing is to make every tab a normal tab stop and delete the arrow
handling — then everything is reachable with Tab like the rest of the page and
there is nothing custom to get wrong." He wants to do it this afternoon.

I do not want to relitigate this in review, so I want the strip fixed properly
now, and I want a short written answer to his proposal that I can paste in the
thread. The module and its green test suite are attached, along with the ticket.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/tabs.js`. `createTabs` and the shape it returns are imported by
   three dashboards, so keep the exported surface working.
2. Add cases to `test/tabs.test.js` that are red against the supplied module and
   green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md`: what was actually wrong, what the strip
   does now key by key, and a direct answer to the proposal in the thread.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/tabs.js`. `createTabs` and the shape it returns are imported by
   three dashboards, so keep the exported surface working.
2. Add cases to `test/tabs.test.js` that are red against the supplied module and
   green after your change. The suite must keep running under `node --test`.
3. Write `docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md`: what was actually wrong, what the strip
   does now key by key, and a direct answer to the proposal in the thread.
assertions: src/tabs.js is edited, test/tabs.test.js gains cases, and docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md exists and addresses the proposal in the thread. Producing the code change with no written answer scores at most half.

attrsFor returns tabindex 0 for the active tab only and -1 for every other tab, so the strip is a single stop in the page's Tab sequence and the arrow keys move within it. Leaving tabindex 0 on all seven scores zero for this criterion regardless of anything else delivered. Emitting -1 on all of them, so the strip cannot be reached by Tab at all, also scores zero. Describing the arrangement in the review document without changing attrsFor scores at most half.

The arrow handling moves DOM focus onto the newly active tab as well as updating aria-selected and the tabindex pair — for example by returning or recording the element id to focus and calling focus on it — and a new test proves focus moved. This is the actual cause of the screen-reader report: the reader announces what has focus, not what carries aria-selected. An answer that changes only aria-selected, exactly as the supplied module already does, scores zero. Moving focus but leaving the tabindex values stale so the browser's own Tab order disagrees scores at most half.

MUST NOT emit tabindex values above 0 anywhere in src/tabs.js. Numbering the tabs 1..7 to control their order creates a focus order separate from the DOM and breaks as soon as tabs are added or reordered. Any positive tabindex in the delivered module scores zero for this criterion.

docs/tabs-keyboard-review.md states plainly that deleting the arrow handling and making every tab a tab stop is not the fix, and why — it is the cause of the support lead's seven presses, and the strip's convention is one stop plus arrows. Adopting the proposal scores zero. Fixing the code correctly but leaving the proposal unanswered, so it comes back in review, scores at most half.
Home moves to the first tab and End to the last, both moving focus the same way the arrows do. Absent entirely scores zero; implemented as selection-only, without focus, scores at most half.

At least one added case fails against src/tabs.js exactly as supplied — a focus assertion and a tabindex assertion are the two that do — and passes after the change, with the suite still running under node --test and no dependency added. Cases that pass against both versions score zero for this criterion. The four supplied tests must still pass; deleting one to make room scores zero.
